entries.title: Preparing clay
entries.summary: Raw clay is gritty and a little too dry to shape. Knead it with a little water until it is smooth and evenly damp.

sections.text: Clay straight from the bank is lumpy, full of grit and a little too dry: shape it like that and it cracks. Kneading - pressing, folding and pressing again - works the grit out and spreads the water evenly through the lump.

steps: Hold raw clay and press [key]E[/key] on a work surface or on bare ground. Up to four lumps from the stack go onto it at once.
Knead: press [key]LMB[/key], drag down and let go to fold. A longer press works the clay harder.
Watch the Moisture gauge; its green band is the sweet spot. Too dry? [key]RMB[/key] splashes in a little water.
Keep kneading until Evenness is nearly full, then press [key]Enter[/key]. You get back as many lumps of prepared clay as you put in.

sections.text: Clay shapes well when it is between about 20% and 31% water. Raw clay comes up at around 17%, depending on how damp the ground was. Each splash is about a hundredth of a liter - a lot for a single lump, not much for four. Kneading in the open air slowly dries the clay, which is also how you rescue clay that is too wet.

Splashes come from the pond if you are working near it - the clay bank is ideal - or from a fired vessel with water in it, carried in your pack. Anywhere else you'll be told there is no water within reach.

list: [b]Too dry[/b] (below about 19%): it cracks and crumbles and hardly improves as you knead. Add water.
[b]Too wet[/b] (above 31%): sticky; kneading does only half as much. Keep kneading to work water out.
[b]Still lumpy[/b]: you can't finish until it is smooth. Knead more.

sections.tip: Changed your mind? Gather up the work ([key]LMB[/key] on it, outside the close-up) and your clay comes back as raw lumps, as damp as you left it.

entries.title: Shaping pottery
entries.summary: Shape prepared clay into a bowl, cup or jar with your hands: open the hollow, pull the walls up, form the rim and smooth it with wet hands.

sections.text: Clay doesn't appear or disappear as you work it - it moves. Pull a wall up and it grows taller and thinner; press a hollow open and the clay you push aside thickens the walls. A lump becomes a vessel by being moved around, not by being added to.

Hold prepared clay and press [key]E[/key] on a work surface or on bare ground. Up to four lumps - a quarter liter each - go onto the work at once; more clay makes a bigger pot. Close up, the clay turns slowly by itself. The [key]Wheel[/key] turns it further, and [key]W[/key] and [key]S[/key] let you look from higher or lower.

list: [b]Wall[/b]: [key]LMB[/key] on the outside and drag. Sideways narrows or widens it at that height; upward pulls the clay up into a taller, thinner wall.
[b]Top[/b]: [key]LMB[/key] on top of the solid lump and drag down to open and deepen a hollow; drag sideways to widen the opening.
[b]Inside wall[/b]: [key]LMB[/key] inside the opening and drag to widen it from within.
[b]Rim[/b]: [key]LMB[/key] on the rim. Drag outward to flare it, or down to press it firm and strong.
[b]Smooth[/b]: hold [key]RMB[/key] and move over the surface. Wet hands even out the walls and smooth away lumps, using a little water from the pond.
[b]Trim[/b]: hold [key]T[/key] and click to cut the top off at that height. Whole lumps' worth of the offcut come back to you as prepared clay.
[b]Add clay[/b]: [key]R[/key] adds another lump of prepared clay from your pack.
Hold [key]Shift[/key] while dragging for fine control.

sections.text: The shape decides the name. A wide, shallow hollow is a [b]bowl[/b]; a deeper one holding up to about 0.9 liters is a [b]cup[/b]; an opening clearly narrower than the belly, on a pot holding at least a quarter liter, makes a [b]jar[/b]. Any other hollow shape is a [b]vessel[/b], and a solid lump stays a clay shape. While you work, the panel shows how much it will hold, how thick the walls and floor are, and gauges for evenness, rim and smoothness.

list: Walls about 6 to 7 millimeters thick. Under 3.5 mm they may crack drying or firing; over about 13 mm they trap water and can burst in the fire.
The same thickness all the way up.
A smooth surface and a firm, pressed rim.
A base wide enough to stand on without tipping.
A floor that isn't pierced - press too deep and the pot will leak.

sections.text: Press [key]Enter[/key] and the wet pot is set down right where you made it, with a few words on how it turned out. It is soft and full of water: let it dry completely before it goes anywhere near a fire. Until you press [key]Enter[/key], you can still gather the work up ([key]LMB[/key] on it, outside the close-up) and get your clay back.

sections.warn: Unfired clay holds no water and doesn't survive rain: soaked, it slumps back into raw clay.

entries.title: Drying
entries.summary: Wet pottery must dry completely before firing. Clay dries in warm, dry, breezy air; rain undoes it, so dry your pots under a roof.

sections.text: A freshly shaped pot is about a quarter water. Heat it like that and the water flashes to steam inside the clay and bursts it. So pottery dries first, slowly, in the air: wet, then leather-hard, then dry. A pot's name and description tell you which, and how much water is left in it.

list: Warm air - afternoons are far better than nights.
Wind, and dry air. When the air turns humid before rain, everything dries slowly.
Sun, if the pot stands out in the open.
Thin walls. A thick-walled pot can take twice as long to dry as one with ordinary walls.

sections.text: Set the pot down to dry - nothing dries in your pack. In fair weather it takes about a day.

Rain soaks unfired clay. A pot that gets too wet loses its shape and slumps back into lumps of raw clay, and the whole island hears about it. Anything with a roof over it is safe from rain - a thatch roof, or any finished building above it.

When the description says bone dry, it is ready: a bone-dry pot never bursts with steam. Anything damper - leather-hard or wet - may. Even a dry pot can still crack from heat that comes on too suddenly, so let the fire build around it.

list: Cut grass cures into straw in about a day in the open.
Wood seasons from green to dry in a day or two.
Lumps of clay left lying dry out too. Raw clay can be kneaded with water back to the right dampness.

sections.tip: Dry pottery under a roof. It dries a little slower out of the sun, but no shower can undo a day's drying.

track.text: Raise a roof to dry it under
Fire it once it is bone dry

entries.title: Firing pottery
entries.summary: Heat turns dry clay into ceramic for good. Pots need a bright red heat - over 550 °C, ideally 750 °C or more - in a fire that heats and cools them gently.

sections.text: Above about 550 °C the clay itself changes: it stops being clay and becomes ceramic - hard, waterproof and permanent. A pot has to soak in that heat for a while: about ten in-game minutes at a bright 750 °C, twice as long at 650 °C, quicker if the fire is hotter still. A pit fire gets there more reliably than an open campfire, and far more gently.

list: [b]Damp clay[/b]: water left in the clay flashes to steam and bursts it. Fire only bone-dry pots - and give them a few extra hours.
[b]Sudden heat[/b]: a pot heated or cooled too fast can crack. Open, windy fires are the worst; a closed-in pit, which heats and cools slowly, protects them.
[b]A weak form[/b]: very thin, very thick or uneven walls and a thin floor all make a pot more likely to crack - even at the very end of a good firing.
[b]Cold water[/b] on a hot pot cracks it as often as not.

steps: Dig a shallow pit with your hands or a digging tool. Its earth walls hold heat in as well as anything can.
Set your bone-dry pots in it with [key]RMB[/key], and pile fuel around and over them: tinder and twigs where you will light it, then sticks and plenty of dry firewood. Charcoal burns hottest of all.
Light it with a burning stick or with the fire drill.
Once it burns well, close it in: stones around the rim, and some earth packed over the top - but leave openings. A fire without air dies, and a sealed one only chars its wood.
Keep it burning hot for a good while, then let it burn down and cool by itself.
When it has cooled, take the pots out. A pot that made it is now called fired: a fired bowl, cup or jar.

sections.text: Hot pottery burns your hands - anything hotter than about 70 °C does. If the prompt says [i]hot![/i], wait. Never cool hot pots with water.
A cracked pot can't be mended and won't hold water. Broken fired pottery - potsherds - holds heat well as part of a firing pit's cover.

sections.tip: Fire several pots at once: they share the same heat. The middle of the fire bed is hottest; pots at the edge may need longer.
